q: Which statement defines usability?
options: General quantitative or qualitative criteria used during testing to establish benchmarks and determine if an interaction is successful
A structured set of procedures that verifies functional system requirements and investigates whether the design is intuitive for target users
A measure of how well a specific user in a specific context can use a product to achieve a defined goal effectively, efficiently, and satisfactorily
The rate at which user performance improves over time across repeated attempts
explanation: Usability measures how well a specific user in a specific context reaches a defined goal effectively, efficiently, and satisfactorily. The first option defines metrics, the second defines testing, and the last defines learnability.

q: Who created the System Usability Scale (SUS), and in what year?
options: John Brooke, 1986
Donald A. Norman, 1986
John Brooke, 1996
Jakob Nielsen, 1990
explanation: The SUS was created by John Brooke in 1986. Norman and Nielsen are usability figures but did not create the SUS, and 1996 is the wrong year.

q: Which pillar of usability asks how well the system prevents errors, minimizes their impact, and helps users recover from mistakes?
options: Effectiveness / Useful
Error Tolerance
Efficiency / Usable
Ease of Learning / Learnability
explanation: Error Tolerance covers preventing errors, limiting their impact, and supporting recovery. Effectiveness concerns accurate task completion, Efficiency concerns speed and effort for experienced users, and Learnability concerns first-time users.

q: Which description matches the structure of the System Usability Scale?
options: 10 standardized items scored on a 7-point Likert scale from 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 7 (Strongly Agree)
12 standardized items scored on a 5-point Likert scale from 1 (Strongly Agree) to 5 (Strongly Disagree)
5 standardized items scored on a 10-point rating scale from 1 (Very Poor) to 10 (Excellent)
10 standardized items scored on a 5-point Likert scale from 1 (Strongly Disagree) to 5 (Strongly Agree)
explanation: The SUS has 10 standardized items on a 5-point Likert scale where 1 is Strongly Disagree and 5 is Strongly Agree. The other options change the item count, the scale length, or reverse the anchors.

q: In measuring task success, what is partial success?
options: A graded completion score based on whether minor slips occurred or facilitator assistance was needed
A result with only two outcomes: the task is completed unassisted or is a complete failure
The percentage of total participants who completed the task
The time spent before participants abandon the task or run out of time
explanation: Partial success gives a graded score depending on minor slips or facilitator help. Two outcomes only is binary success, a percentage of participants is how task success is tracked overall, and time before abandoning is failed task time.

q: Which three subscales do participants use to evaluate a system with semantic differential bipolar adjectives?
options: Creativity, Function, and Control
Pleasure, Arousal, and Dominance
Creativity, Function, and Comfort
Usefulness, Satisfaction, and Ease of Use
explanation: The three primary psychological dimensions are Creativity, Function, and Comfort. Control is not a subscale (Easy to control is only an anchor in Comfort), and the other two sets belong to different rating instruments.

q: Which term refers to the mental effort spent deciding what action to take?
options: Physical Efficiency
Cognitive Efficiency
Learnability
Time on Task
explanation: Cognitive efficiency is the mental effort of deciding what to do. Physical efficiency counts actions such as clicks and keystrokes, learnability is improvement over time, and time on task is the duration of the task.

q: Which SUS score is given as corresponding to the 90th percentile, Grade A?
explanation: A score of 80.3 corresponds to the 90th percentile, Grade A. A score of 68 is the industry average benchmark, and 85 and 50 are not the cited percentile example.

q: Which type of error arises from incorrect mental models or misleading UI cues?
options: Mistakes
Slips
Misclicks
Backtracking
explanation: Mistakes come from a wrong mental model or misleading interface cues. Slips are unintentional errors made when the goal was correct, while misclicks and backtracking are behaviors logged in behavior tracking.

q: Which focus area of issue-based metrics involves distinguishing between normal user exploration and genuine usability defects?
options: Behavior Tracking
Identification
Usability Questions
Apriori Coding
explanation: Identification separates normal exploration from real defects. Behavior tracking documents hesitations and misclicks, usability questions log moments of confusion, and apriori coding belongs to qualitative analysis of self-reported data.

q: Which set lists examples of what physical efficiency measures?
options: Hesitations, misclicks, backtracking, and frustration
Sighs, posture changes, and facial expressions
Keystrokes, clicks, and mouse travel distance
Comments, questions, and self-talk
explanation: Physical efficiency counts the physical actions needed, such as keystrokes, clicks, and mouse travel distance. The other sets are behavior tracking items, non-verbal behaviors, and verbal behaviors.

q: Which self-reported data collection method has the drawback of requiring manual data entry into analysis software?
options: Oral
Online
Moderated remote
Written
explanation: Written paper-based surveys must be typed into analysis software. Oral collection requires detailed manual notes, online collection gathers data automatically, and moderated remote is a testing format, not a survey collection method.

q: Which rating format presents pairs of opposite adjectives and has participants mark their perception along a continuum between the two anchors?
options: Likert Scales
Semantic Differential Scales
Top-2 / Bottom-2 Analysis
System Usability Scale
explanation: Semantic differential scales use bipolar adjective pairs with a continuum between them. Likert scales measure level of agreement with statements, top-2 / bottom-2 is an analysis method, and the SUS is a 10-item Likert-based survey.

q: What is the term for defining a codebook of themes or keywords prior to analysis based on research goals?
options: Apriori Coding
Thematic Grouping
Open-Ended Questions
Video Coding
explanation: Apriori coding means setting up the codebook before analysis. Thematic grouping applies those codes and groups them into themes, open-ended questions collect the raw commentary, and video coding is used to observe non-verbal behavior.

q: Which sequence gives the 4 usability testing steps in the correct order?
options: Recruit Testers, Planning, Set User Tasks, Facilitate / Moderate Testing
Planning, Recruit Testers, Set User Tasks, Facilitate / Moderate Testing
Planning, Set User Tasks, Recruit Testers, Facilitate / Moderate Testing
Set User Tasks, Planning, Facilitate / Moderate Testing, Recruit Testers
explanation: The steps are Planning, Set User Tasks, Recruit Testers, and Facilitate / Moderate Testing. The other sequences move recruiting or task setting out of place.

q: Which sequence correctly describes how a SUS score is calculated?
options: Add all 10 raw scores, multiply the sum by 2.5, then subtract 1 from odd items and subtract even items from 5
Subtract 1 from even items and subtract odd items from 5, add the 10 converted scores, then multiply the sum by 2.5
Multiply each raw score by 2.5, convert the odd and even items, then add the 10 results
Subtract 1 from odd items and subtract even items from 5, add the 10 converted scores, then multiply the sum by 2.5
explanation: Odd items become raw minus 1, even items become 5 minus raw, the 10 converted scores are summed (0 to 40), and the sum is multiplied by 2.5 to give 0 to 100. The second option swaps the odd and even rules, and the others convert at the wrong stage.

q: Which bias is the tendency of participants to give overly positive feedback during in-person or phone sessions to avoid offending the researcher?
options: Selection Bias
Social Desirability Bias
Reporting Bias
Moderator Bias
explanation: Social desirability bias is being overly positive to avoid offending the researcher. Selection bias comes from a non-representative sample, reporting bias is selectively revealing or hiding information, and moderator bias comes from the moderator's demeanor and hints.

q: What is the name of the effect in which the test monitor's expectations subconsciously influence participant responses?
options: Observer-Expectancy Effect
Social Desirability Bias
Reporting Bias
Feedback Tendency
explanation: The Observer-Expectancy Effect is prevented by separating the survey collector from the facilitator. Social desirability and reporting bias come from the participant, and feedback tendency is how vocal a participant is.

q: After open-ended comments have been collected, which sequence correctly orders their qualitative analysis?
options: Tag keywords, define the apriori codebook, then group the tagged keywords into themes
Group comments into themes, tag keywords, then define the apriori codebook
Define the apriori codebook, group comments into themes, then tag keywords
Define the apriori codebook, tag keywords in the transcripts with the codes, then group them into themes
explanation: The codebook is defined before analysis, then thematic grouping parses the transcripts, tags keywords with the apriori codes, and groups them into usability themes. Tagging or grouping before the codebook exists breaks the method.

q: What does skin conductance, or galvanic skin response (GSR), measure?
options: Real-time cognitive load, engagement, and mental fatigue
Fixation duration, gaze pathways, and visual attention density
Physiological arousal, stress, and cognitive workload
Physical tension through mouse and touchscreen pressure mapping
explanation: GSR measures physiological arousal, stress, and cognitive workload. The first option describes EEG, the second describes eye tracking, and the last describes posture and pressure sensing.

q: Which usability testing step involves conducting sessions, guiding participants, logging behaviors, and administering surveys, and where does it fall in the sequence?
options: Facilitate / Moderate Testing, the fourth and final step
Recruit Testers, the third step
Planning, the first step
Set User Tasks, the second step
explanation: Facilitate / Moderate Testing is the fourth and last step, where sessions are run and surveys administered. Planning defines scope and metrics, Set User Tasks creates scenario-based tasks, and Recruit Testers sources matching participants.

q: Which type of metric focuses on identifying visual, structural, or logical defects in the interface through direct observation of participant behavior?
options: Performance metrics
Issue-based metrics
Self-reported metrics
Behavioral and psychological metrics
explanation: Issue-based metrics find defects in the interface by observing participants. Performance metrics quantify success, time, and errors, self-reported metrics capture subjective opinions, and behavioral and psychological metrics capture physiological and behavioral signals.

q: Which pairing of an issue-based bias category and an example is mismatched?
options: Participant bias: testing with too few or non-representative participants
Method bias: differences in logging tools or note-taking practices
Environment bias: noise levels and external interruptions
Artifact bias: the moderator's body language and subtle verbal hints
explanation: Body language and verbal hints are moderator biases. Artifact biases come from the thing being tested, such as bugs, latency, prototype fidelity, or missing backend features. The other three pairings are correct.

q: Which statement about the pillars of usability is NOT true?
options: Effectiveness / Useful asks whether users can complete their tasks accurately and achieve their goals
Engagement / Used asks how pleasant, satisfying, and engaging the interface is
Efficiency / Usable asks how easily first-time users accomplish basic tasks when they first encounter the design
Usability is measured continuously throughout the entire product development lifecycle
explanation: Efficiency concerns how quickly and with how little effort users perform tasks once they know the system. First-time use is Ease of Learning / Learnability. The other statements are correct.

q: A participant intends to press Submit on a form but accidentally presses the Cancel button next to it. How should this error be classified?
options: A slip, because the goal was correct but the action was unintentional
A mistake, because the participant's mental model of the form was incorrect
A partial success, because a facilitator had to give assistance
A reporting bias, because the participant suppressed information
explanation: The participant had the right goal and simply made an unintended action, which is a slip. A mistake would require a wrong mental model or misleading cue, and partial success and reporting bias do not describe the error itself.

q: Which statement about self-reported and behavioral data is NOT true?
options: Top-2 / Bottom-2 analysis focuses on the percentage of responses in the two most positive versus the two most negative categories
Think-aloud protocols are used to capture non-verbal behaviors such as sighs and posture changes
Making surveys completely anonymous helps reduce social desirability bias
Behavioral and psychological metrics capture objective physiological and behavioral data
explanation: Think-aloud protocols capture verbal behaviors such as comments, questions, and self-talk. Non-verbal behaviors like sighs and posture changes need direct observation or video coding. The other statements are correct.

q: Which pairing of a testing format and its description is mismatched?
options: In-person testing: a lab setting allowing maximum control and high-fidelity biometric data capture
Remote testing: moderated or unmoderated sessions over video software in the user's natural environment
Oral data collection: the easiest method for capturing quick immediate ratings
Guerrilla testing: formal, scheduled lab sessions with recruited participants matching target personas
explanation: Guerrilla testing is informal, rapid testing with ad-hoc participants in public settings, not formal lab sessions. The other three pairings are correct.

q: Which statement about the System Usability Scale is NOT true?
options: A SUS score of 68 means that 68 percent of participants found the system usable
Odd-numbered items are positively worded and even-numbered items are negatively worded
The sum of the converted scores ranges from 0 to 40 before it is multiplied by 2.5
A score below 68 indicates below-average usability with significant usability issues
explanation: 68 is the industry average benchmark on a 0 to 100 composite scale, not a percentage of users. The other statements correctly describe SUS item wording, the converted range, and interpretation.

q: During a test, the evaluator instructs users to click Menu, then Settings, then Profile, instead of giving a realistic goal, so their natural navigation is never observed. Which bias category does this fall under?
options: Participant bias
Task bias
Method bias
Environment bias
explanation: Rigid step-by-step instructions versus open-ended scenario goals is a task bias (defined vs. open-ended). Participant bias concerns who is tested, method bias concerns devices and data handling, and environment bias concerns the room.

q: A participant answers 4 on every odd-numbered SUS item and 1 on every even-numbered SUS item. What is the SUS score?
explanation: Each odd item converts to $4 - 1 = 3$, so five give $15$. Each even item converts to $5 - 1 = 4$, so five give $20$. The sum is $35$, and $35 \times 2.5 = 87.5$. The value 62.5 skips the conversion, 35 skips the multiplication, and 37.5 subtracts 1 from every item.
